Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP Australian politics Anne Aly reveals she has received 19 death threats in the last week alone After an opposition MP says she should be ‘shamed and stoned’, the federal minister hits back at ‘racist and misogynistic’ language Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast Ben Doherty Tue 13 Oct 2026 05.13 EDT Last modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 05.59 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Anne Aly has condemned as “racist” and “misogynistic” comments in parliament calling for her to be “stoned in the square” – while revealing she has received 19 death threats in the last week alone. The Gold Coast Liberal National MP Angie Bell, the member for Moncrieff, told the House of Representatives that Aly, the small business minister, and the prime minister should be “shamed and stoned in the square” over a decision made by the tax office. Bell was forced to withdraw the comment by the speaker. Vikki Campion, News Corp columnist and wife of Barnaby Joyce, begins role with NSW One Nation Read more On Instagram, Aly responded with an emotive post-to-camera, saying she had been the subject of consistent death threats, including previous threats that she should be stoned. “I don’t usually comment about these sorts of things, but I feel like I have to. This past week alone, I’ve had 19 death threats on my social media. And in the past I’ve had death threats that are couched in that exact same language: stone her.” Aly said that the comments directed at her were not just unparliamentary, but fundamentally inimical to Australian values. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here “We are a country that proudly stands against violence against women and against regimes that use brutal methods like stoning against women. “This is not just something that we should just turn away from. “It is racist. It is misogynistic. And it is something that should never have been said.” Bell made the remarks before question time on Tuesday as part of an opposition attack on the government over the Australian Taxation Office’s decision to ban credit card payments used to pay tax bills. Bell said millions of Australians were employed by small businesses, and would be harmed by the decision. “This minister and this prime minister should be absolutely shamed and stoned in the square,” she said. Bell was forced by the speaker to withdraw the comments after the government’s leader of the house, Tony Burke, raised concerns with what he said was “physically violent imagery”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Politics, really Our political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for you after newsletter promotion Australia – like other liberal democracies – has experienced a dramatic rise in threats against politicians and other public figures. More than 50 police reports on a range of alleged criminal offences were made during the last federal election campaign and the Australian federal police received 951 referrals or threats against parliamentarians in the 2024-25 financial year, an increase of more than 60% in just four years. Last year, the then AFP commissioner, Reece Kershaw, told Senate estimates that female politicians were particular targets, and that “the nature of threats and comments directed at female parliamentarians and high officeholders is particularly troubling, with a common feature being offensive material centred on derogatory language about their appearance”. “Some of this material also contains extremely violent themes, including threats of graphic, sexual violence,” he said. “These threats, which are being made online or are being sent in the post or over the phone, are sometimes also directed at their children.” Kershaw said politicians were targeted because of their public profiles, or because of their policy positions. “However, in some cases, it appears male offenders are targeting women because they are women. Composite: PA UK news Man accused of sexually assaulting woman drugged by husband says he thought it was ‘their kink’ Two of four men on trial say they met couple via online ads and swinging website and had no idea wife had been drugged Steven Morris Fri 30 Oct 2026 14.06 EDT Last modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 14.29 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Men accused of sexually assaulting a woman whose then husband drugged her for years and allowed her to be abused have described being invited to the couple’s home via online adverts and a swinging website. One of those accused of assaulting Joanne Young, who has waived her legal right to anonymity, as she lay restrained and blindfolded said he was a young man “trying out things” and had no idea she was drugged. A second said there was a large “cuckold community” of men who watched their wives having sex, claiming his encounter was “just a sex meet” and she seemed “fine”. Philip Young, 50, has pleaded guilty to multiple charges of drugging and sexually abusing his former wife, 49, at their home in Swindon, Wiltshire, over a number of years. The prosecution has said he advertised his wife online and “loaned” her out to other men. Four other men are on trial at Winchester crown court, including Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, of Swindon, who denies sexual assault by penetration and sexual touching in June 2016. In police interviews read out to the jury, Sanderson-Doyle said he contacted Philip Young via Craigslist after seeing an ad in its adult section for a woman tied and blindfolded. He said he thought he had met a couple “trying to live out whatever their kink is”. He said he went to the Youngs’ house on his motorcycle. He asked if he should take his shoes off when he arrived, but kept his balaclava on throughout. He saw there were toys in the house so assumed the couple had children. Sanderson-Doyle, then 21, said he found Joanne Young “tied up and blindfolded” as she had been pictured in the online ad. She did not say anything but seemed awake. The defendant said that at one point he heard her say “No” but he thought she wanted him to do something different rather than stop completely. Sanderson-Doyle told police he started to get a “vibe she wasn’t enjoying it or was not comfortable” and left soon afterwards. He continued: “I thought I had her consent. I didn’t know she was drugged,” adding: “I was just a young guy trying out things.” He called the encounter a “non event”. A second man, Norman Macksoni, 48, of Sharnbrook, Bedfordshire, denies one count of rape in February 2017. He told police he worked as an MC and went by the username “dark stranger” on the swingers’ site where he made contact with Philip Young. He said the site was “about couples living out fantasies” and there was a thriving “cuckold community”. Macksoni told police he had never had sex without consent and Joanne Young was “totally coherent”. He said: “It was just a sex meet and then I left.” The defendant told officers he did not wear a condom and added: “He specifically said she didn’t like them.” Also on trial are Richard Wilkins, 62, of Toothill, Wiltshire, who has pleaded not guilty to one count of rape and one of assault by penetration, and Mohammed Hassan, 38, of Swindon, who has pleaded not guilty to one count of sexual touching. https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/new.text: New Delhi, India and the Czech Republic are looking to expand defence industrial cooperation, with a focus on technology collaboration, manufacturing capabilities and stronger industrial partnerships. The development provides a wider context for growing cooperation between Indian and Czech companies in the defence manufacturing sector.India and the Czech Republic have been exploring opportunities to strengthen defence industrial relations through technology sharing, joint production, research and development, and capacity building. The India-Czech Joint Defence Committee provides a platform for discussions on existing cooperation and potential areas for further engagement.VTDS and DEUS Automation PartnershipAgainst this backdrop, the technology partnership between Vijayan Trishul Defence Solutions (VTDS) and DEUS Automation a.s., a sister company of the Czech STV Group, highlights the growing role of industrial collaboration in strengthening India's domestic defence manufacturing capabilities.Industry-level ties have also picked up. In August, Vijayan Trishul Defence Solutions (VTDS), which holds a Home Ministry licence to manufacture small arms and ammunition, signed a technology partnership with DEUS Automation, a sister company of the Czech STV Group, under which the Czech firm will supply technology to produce small-calibre ammunition in India.The partnership brings together VTDS's domestic manufacturing ambitions and DEUS Automation's technological expertise, supporting efforts to develop local production capabilities and strengthen industrial cooperation between the two countries.Leadership and Industry CollaborationVTDS is represented by Mr. Sahil Luthra, Founder and Managing Director, and Ms. Prikansha Luthra, Co-Founder and Director.DEUS Automation a.s. is represented by Mr. Alex Černý, Chief Executive Officer and Member of the Board, and Mr. Ondřej Černý, Manager of Sales, Projects & Purchase.The partnership reflects the contribution that company-level collaborations can make towards strengthening industrial ties between India and the Czech Republic, particularly in areas involving technology transfer and domestic manufacturing.Expanding India-Czech Defence CooperationAs India continues to strengthen its domestic defence production capabilities, international technology partnerships can help build local manufacturing expertise and expand industrial capacity.The VTDS-DEUS Automation partnership illustrates how collaboration between companies can complement broader bilateral efforts to deepen defence industrial relations and promote technological cooperation between India and the Czech Republic.
